Title: Heybrain: The governed AI brain for people and agents. | Product Hunt
## The governed AI brain for people and agents. HeyBrain is your company's shared AI brain for people and agents. Your knowledge is scattered across Slack, Notion, Drive, GitHub and the rest of your stack. Brain connects it into one governed place where your team and your AI agents ask questions and get answers from only what they're allowed to see — same context, same permissions, every access written to a tamper-evident, content-blind log. One company brain: always on, permission-aware, and built for how teams actually use AI. Today we’re launching HeyBrain, one shared company brain that your people and AI agents can work from together. Our company knowledge was everywhere: Slack, Notion, Google Drive, GitHub, docs, conversations, and inside the heads of different people. How do you give AI access to everything your company knows without giving it access to everything? “Can you prove exactly what the AI had access to when it gave this answer?”. That is what we built Brain to solve. Brain sits between your company knowledge and the AI tools your team already uses. It checks who is asking, retrieves only the information that person or agent is cleared to access, and creates a tamper-evident, content-blind record of every access. Connect the tools your company already works in, including Slack, GitHub, Google Drive, Notion, Box, Confluence and Salesforce, and Brain becomes a persistent company memory that both humans and agents can query under the same permissions. Give your company one shared AI memory. Brain checks identity and permissions on every request, so people and agents only retrieve what they are cleared to see. Claude, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents can work from the same governed company context as your team. ChainGPT became the first company running its knowledge through Brain, and it gave us a very clear view of where this category needs to go. Agents increasingly need access to the same context your employees use every day. Shared by people and agents. @ceoguy This governed AI brain idea is great; it solves the permission problem that many companies struggle with when using AI. @ceoguy Shared company knowledge is a great idea.

Title: Sequna: Work memory for AI agents | Product Hunt
# Sequna. ## Work memory for AI agents. Install Sequna in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf, or any MCP-compatible agent. It captures meaningful progress, organizes work under durable goals, auto-runs safe inbox items, and gives you a structured daily review. Launch tags:Productivity•Task Management•Analytics. CloudflareStill paying to deploy your apps? Try Cloudflare Workers for free. No reviews yetBe the first to leave a review for Sequna. Hi everyone — I built Sequna because I kept running into the same problem with AI coding agents: they were great at helping with the current task, but terrible at preserving the actual work thread across sessions. Meaningful progress got buried in chats. End-of-day review was basically manual reconstruction. Sequna is my attempt to fix that. It gives AI agents a work memory layer: - capture meaningful progress - organize work under durable goals - auto-run safe inbox items - generate a structured daily review It is designed for people already using Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf, or other MCP-compatible agents in real workflows. What I most want feedback on: 1. Is “work memory” a clear way to describe the product? 2. Which part feels most valuable: progress capture, goal organization, inbox auto-run, or daily review? 3. Where does the current setup still feel too heavy? This feels relevant for anyone who uses AI agents for real project work instead of one-off prompts. Once you’re juggling goals, follow-ups, and unfinished threads, you need something more structured than chat history. @sherychen That’s exactly the problem I wanted to solve. For one-off prompts, chat history is usually enough. But once the work stretches across multiple sessions, goals, and follow-ups, the thread starts to break down fast. Sequna is built for that longer-running mode of working, where the agent needs to retain meaningful progress instead of just remembering the current conversation. I’m especially interested in whether that framing resonates: not “better chat history,” but a real work memory layer for agent-driven workflows.

An agent walks into a repeat problem like it's the first time, every time. Most memory tools treat everything as disconnected text chunks in a vector store, so nothing carries over, not the reasoning, not the context, not what actually happened last time. Context, who, what, when, why, and how, is stamped on every commit, so retrieval actually means something later. And because it's built directly on ApertureDB (aperturedata.io), the unified graph-vector-multimodal database already running in production, it works the same whether your agents are text-only today or need images, documents, video, or structured records tomorrow. This version of Nexus is built around that: a place for whatever reasoning is already happening to commit, retrieve, and build on, rather than introducing a competing reasoning layer of its own. The thinking behind it: Introducing Aperture Nexus: Multimodal Memory and where existing memory tools fall short. We also started a podcast on this exact question, The Cognitive Layer: Episode 1, with a Netflix engineering lead on trustworthy AI memory. Sounds really interesting, and I saw this as someone who's build / abandoned (not quite abandoned but rather rolled into a different product) a memory tool in the past for AI. It makes a lot of sense to let people incorporate any model/reasoning layer they want, and focusing more on enhancing the infrastructure around it and playing to the strengths of Aperture as a multimodal DB.

results.content:
Title: Graft AI: Turn company operations into a living map for agents | Product Hunt
# Graft AI. ## Turn company operations into a living map for agents. It learns how the work gets done, turns it into a living operational map, and gives agents stable tools with permissions, approvals, audit trails, and verification built in. When the underlying UI changes, Graft detects the drift and repairs the workflow without breaking the agent interface. Hey PH 👋 I started Graft after realizing that the hardest part of deploying agents at work is not the model. It is the software around it. Real companies run on ERPs, desktop apps, internal portals, spreadsheets, and years of operational knowledge that agents cannot reliably understand or use. Graft began as a way to turn those interfaces into stable tools for agents. While building it, the idea grew into something bigger: a living map of how a company actually works. Graft learns the workflow, decisions, permissions, exceptions, and success conditions, then gives agents a safe way to do the work with approvals, audit trails, and verification built in. We are launching early because we want to learn from the people actually building and operating agents. Graft watches real workflow executions and compares decisions, exceptions, and outcomes against the current map; when something changes, it proposes a clear diff, tests it in shadow mode, and only asks for review when the change is risky or uncertain. This is not an agent, its an infra running to understand how your company operates, connects to software your company uses, extracts the domain knowledge from people to create a operating knowledge map (with our advanced memory systems) usable by agents consistently. For example it understands how refunds work, so this won't save it as a doc, it'll see how it functions in your company and map it out, next time something changes it'll update itself. It is deeply integrated to your system and connected to the tools you use and is like an evolving brain. if you're interested and want to talk, you can sign up for the waitlist at graft.axcelner.com. If you're interested and want to talk, sign up for the waitlist at graft.axcelner.com, let me know if you have any questions.
